answer.summary: Lord says frontier-model builders need high-quality data above all, at scale and delivered quickly, plus help assessing whether it improves models and adapting data to their training needs. Quality matters because bad training data is hard to overcome; volume and speed let researchers test hypotheses and expand promising pipelines.

sections.heading: What providers need to deliver
sections.content: Lord identifies three priorities: quality first, then volume and speed. Builders need thousands of high-quality examples in advanced domains such as chemistry, mathematics, and physics. For example, his company recruits top-GPA students from Stanford, Berkeley, and MIT for physics data. It must also turn work around in days, so builders can scale a promising data pipeline while dropping experiments that show no improvement.

sections.heading: Why it matters and what support entails
sections.content: Poor-quality data can be extremely challenging to overcome, much like teaching a student with the wrong material. Builders run experiments on hypotheses for improving models; quick delivery of substantial, high-quality data helps them expand a pipeline once it shows gains. Providers can support this by assessing data at the unit level, approximating whether it improves a capability, and working directly with researchers on how to train with it. Lord says his company has its own research and post-training teams and rents GPUs for this work. He also notes builders want evolving data formats and use cases, including real-world tool-use and trajectory-based data.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately attributes Lord’s three priorities—high-quality data, large volumes in advanced domains, and fast turnaround—to him. It explains that bad data is difficult for models to overcome, while speed helps researchers test hypotheses and scale pipelines that show gains. These points are supported by the cited transcript excerpts.
